HISTORY · TECHNOLOGY · CIVIL LIBERTIES

How the Iraq War affected digital privacy rights

During the War on Terror, the government gained new ways to collect information about people. With the establishment of the PATRIOT Act, data privacy rights in the United States were forever changed.

You can see which numbers were in touch, even without hearing the conversation.

A STUDENT EXPLAINERHISTORICAL FOCUS: 2001–2015VIEW THE SOURCES

OVERVIEW

What does the Iraq War
have to do with privacy?

To understand privacy during the Iraq War, we also have to look at the government’s wider response to 9/11 and rising Middle East tensions.

In Iraq, U.S. forces expanded their use of fingerprints and iris scans to identify people. At home, officials used concurrently expanded surveillance systems to collect records and communications. Both were part of the War on Terror, though they worked under different rules (PCLOB, 2014b, p. 1; U.S. Government Accountability Office [GAO], 2008b, p. 7).

First, the dates: the PATRIOT Act passed in October 2001. The invasion of Iraq began in March 2003. The law was already in place when the war began (Office of the Historian, n.d.; USA PATRIOT Act, 2001).

THE MAIN IDEA

The Iraq War exacerbated what the government could collect, who it could share it with, and what it could do with the records.

2001–2015

What changed,
and when?

Pick a year to see how the laws and the war fit into the same timeline.

2001
OCTOBER 26, 2001

The PATRIOT Act expands surveillance powers.

Section 215 gave the government a way to obtain records for certain investigations. Officials later relied on it to justify collecting phone records in bulk. A majority of the oversight board said the law didn’t support that use (PCLOB, 2014b, pp. 8–10; USA PATRIOT Act, 2001, § 215).

The Act passed before the 2003 invasion, as part of the wider response to 9/11.

Read the original Act

SURVEILLANCE LAWS

What information
could be collected?

A record of a call and a recording of the conversation tell you different things. The government collected them under different programs.

PATRIOT ACT · SECTION 215

Phone records
without the conversation

The NSA used court orders under Section 215 to collect phone records in bulk. Those records didn’t contain recordings of conversations. In 2014, a 3–2 majority of the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board said the law didn’t support the program and recommended ending it (PCLOB, 2014b, pp. 16, 21–22).

The privacy issue

The records showed which numbers called each other, when, and how long the calls lasted. Those patterns could reveal relationships even without hearing the conversation (PCLOB, 2014b, pp. 21–22, 157).

FISA AMENDMENTS ACT · SECTION 702

When a foreign target
talks to an American

Under the 2008 law, intelligence agencies could collect foreign intelligence by targeting people reasonably believed to be non-U.S. persons abroad. If those targets were talking to Americans, those exchanges could be collected too (FISA Amendments Act, 2008, § 101; PCLOB, 2014a, p. 114). This was a different program from bulk phone-record collection.

The privacy issue

Your messages could be collected because of who you were talking to, even if you weren’t the target.

This section covers 2001–2015. It explains what happened then; it isn’t a guide to the law today.

PRIMARY SOURCE

Read the
PATRIOT Act

Section 215 allowed the government to seek records and other tangible items for certain investigations (USA PATRIOT Act, 2001, § 215).

The argument came later, over whether this section allowed bulk phone-record collection. Reading the law helps separate what Congress passed from what officials later argued it allowed (PCLOB, 2014b, pp. 8–10).

Biometric databases

In Iraq and Afghanistan, U.S. forces used fingerprints, iris images, and photos of faces to identify people. The steps below show how those records could be used (GAO, 2008a, p. 2).

Collecting someone’s data

ACADEMIC PERSPECTIVE

Being identified could
affect where you could go.

A record can have real consequences when someone uses it to decide whether you’re a threat.

In her peer-reviewed article, Stefka Hristova argues that biometric systems in Iraq helped officials sort people into groups they saw as friendly or threatening. A scan could become part of a decision about someone’s freedom to move (Hristova, 2014, pp. 516–517).

That’s Hristova’s reading of what these systems did. A match can help establish identity; it can’t tell you what someone intends to do or whether they’re guilty.

Read the peer-reviewed article

WHY THIS MATTERS

What this means
for digital privacy

This history gives us a reason to ask who has access to our information and what they’re allowed to do with it.

Who’s collecting the information?+

The Section 215 debate raises a basic question: how much information should the government be able to collect about people who aren’t suspected of wrongdoing? It also matters who gets to approve that collection (PCLOB, 2014b, pp. 21–22).

What can they do with it?+

Identifying someone, investigating them, and deciding they’re a threat are different things. Hristova’s Iraq case shows how a record can become part of a much bigger judgment about a person (Hristova, 2014, pp. 516–517).

Can the rules change?+

Yes. The 2015 USA FREEDOM Act ended the Section 215 bulk phone-record program. Its replacement used specific identifiers and records held by phone companies. That changed one program; other forms of surveillance continued (Office of the Director of National Intelligence, 2015, p. 1; USA FREEDOM Act, 2015, §§ 101, 103, 109).
